status: UNPUBLISHED partial editorial/art draft; not registered in app
sourceReview: Read all bundled BSB Psalm 22, Psalm 71, Matthew 27 and John 19 before writing this group. Psalm 71 supplies a separate prayer recalling dependence from birth; John 19 supplies a later Gospel account of thirst, not a claim that it explicitly quotes Psalm 22:15 or 16. Animal imagery does not identify the psalm’s unnamed human opponents.

verses.title: Secure from the beginning
verses.heading: The speaker returns from the mockers’ words to remembered care
verses.meaning: Yet turns the prayer away from the mockers’ taunt and back toward God. The speaker recalls birth and security at a mother’s breast as signs of care before any conscious achievement or declaration of trust. This personal recollection answers ridicule with remembered dependence; it does not report that the present danger has disappeared. The verse names the speaker’s own mother without describing her life or identifying a particular family scene. Readers whose early care was painful or absent need not pretend otherwise to enter the lament. The remembered security gives this speaker a reason to ask for help now.
verses.contextTitle: A change of voice after the quoted taunt
verses.context: Verse 8 reports what the mockers say about the sufferer. Verse 9 resumes direct address to God, and verse 10 continues the memory of dependence from birth. Psalm 71:5–6 recalls a similar lifelong reliance within a separate prayer that later voices the vulnerability of old age.
explore: Yet You
The speaker addresses God again. This is the sufferer’s appeal, distinct from the third-person ridicule quoted in verse 8.
Made me secure
The memory begins with received care rather than earned strength. The anonymous mother and wrapped infant are symbolic art, not a portrait of the speaker’s actual family.
verses.reflect: What memory of care, however small or recent, could you bring into a difficult prayer? What support would help if early memories offer little comfort?
verses.alt: A fully clothed anonymous mother cradles a wrapped infant beneath an olive tree in a quiet imagined courtyard.

verses.title: You have been my God
verses.heading: Dependence reaches back beyond the speaker’s earliest choices
verses.meaning: The prayer continues to look back to birth, describing a life entrusted to God from its beginning. Cast upon You expresses dependence, while You have been my God names an enduring relationship. The verse does not describe a baby consciously choosing a belief or establish a ritual that readers must reconstruct. Its force comes from the contrast between lifelong reliance and the speaker’s present feeling that God is far away. Remembering that relationship prepares the urgent request of verse 11. The painting’s cradle illustrates vulnerability without making God visible as a parent or a human guardian.
verses.contextTitle: Remembered relationship becomes a present appeal
verses.context: Verses 9–10 form a personal counterpart to the communal memories in verses 4–5. Both recollections stand inside continuing distress. Verse 11 immediately asks for nearness and help, showing that remembered care has not removed the need to lament.
explore: From birth
The repeated beginning of life extends the recollection in verse 9. The text gives no additional childhood episode to narrate.
My God
This personal address also appears in the opening cry. Relationship and the question of abandonment remain together within the same psalm.
verses.reflect: What relationship or source of care has helped carry you through changes in your own strength? What do you need from that relationship today?
verses.alt: A wrapped sleeping infant rests in a woven cradle while an anonymous parent watches from a softly lit doorway.

verses.title: Trouble is near
verses.heading: The prayer asks for nearness in the absence of a helper
verses.meaning: The request is brief and urgent: God must not be far when trouble is close. The speaker sets two kinds of nearness against one another and gives a reason for the appeal: there is no one to help. This describes the sufferer’s isolation in the poem; it is not an instruction to refuse human companionship or practical assistance. The remembered care of verses 9–10 now becomes a plea for care in the present. The verse leaves the trouble unnamed until the surrounding images develop its force. Its direct language can give shape to a prayer when a person has little energy for explanation.
verses.contextTitle: A hinge between remembered care and surrounding threats
verses.context: Verse 11 follows the recollection of dependence from birth. Verses 12–18 then describe encircling threats and bodily distress before verse 19 repeats the request that God not be far off. Psalm 71:12 makes a similar appeal within its own account of accusers and failing strength.
explore: Be not far
The plea returns to the distance named in verse 1. It asks for help without pretending that the speaker already experiences relief.
No one to help
The statement intensifies the speaker’s vulnerability. It makes the need for support audible rather than making isolation a spiritual ideal.
verses.reflect: Where do you most need someone to come alongside you? Could one short, specific request make that need easier for another person to understand?
verses.alt: A solitary anonymous adult follows a rocky path beneath a limestone ledge above a broad shadowed valley.

verses.title: Surrounded by strength
verses.heading: Bull imagery conveys the power of encircling threats
verses.meaning: The poem depicts danger through many bulls and strong bulls of Bashan surrounding the speaker. The repeated enclosure gives force to the isolation named in verse 11: powerful threats seem to occupy every direction. The animal language should be read alongside verse 16, which explicitly names a band of evil men. It does not establish that an actual herd attacked the speaker, identify the opponents, or supply an incident from David’s life. Bashan belongs to the verse’s wording, but the study does not invent an ancient landscape or event to explain it. The painting keeps the bulls as a symbolic image of intimidating strength.
verses.contextTitle: The first of several surrounding animal images
verses.context: Bulls in verse 12 lead to lion-like jaws in verse 13 and dogs in verse 16. Verse 21 later returns to the lion and wild oxen in the plea for rescue. These related images trace the perceived danger without revealing the identities of the opponents.
explore: Surround me
The spatial image repeats as encircle me. Its emotional force comes from the speaker’s sense of being hemmed in, with no helper nearby.
Strong bulls of Bashan
The named place remains in the exact Scripture. The notes explain the threatening strength expressed here without adding an unverified historical scene.
verses.reflect: What feels overpowering or difficult to escape right now? Is there one part of that pressure you could name clearly to someone you trust?
verses.alt: Powerful dark bulls form a wide arc around an empty patch of pale earth in a rocky upland field.

verses.title: Jaws opened against me
verses.heading: The threatening figures become a lion comparison
verses.meaning: The surrounding figures open their jaws against the speaker like lions that roar and maul. The explicit comparison makes the danger feel active and close: these are not merely impressive animals observed at a distance. The poem gives voice to the experience of being threatened without identifying a particular attack or permitting the reader to name a group as inherently beastlike. The study’s lion illustration represents this poetic comparison and does not depict a literal encounter from the speaker’s biography. Later verse 21 will return to the lion’s mouth in a plea that reaches toward an answer.
verses.context: Verse 13 develops the bulls’ encirclement into an image of open jaws. Verse 14 then shifts attention to the speaker’s own body and heart. Reading the sequence keeps the animal comparison connected to the lament’s account of vulnerability.
explore: Like lions
The comparison conveys fierce danger. It does not identify a literal species of attacker or tell readers who the unnamed opponents were.
Roar and maul
The verbs intensify the threatening scene. The watercolor conveys that force through a lion’s posture without showing an attack or injured person.
verses.reflect: When another person’s hostility feels overwhelming, what helps you put the experience into words? Who could help you seek room to breathe and support?
verses.alt: A lion stands on a limestone outcrop with its jaws open above a shadowed ravine, without a person or attack.

verses.title: Poured out like water
verses.heading: Water, bones and melting wax express the depth of distress
verses.meaning: The lament turns inward through a series of bodily images: poured-out water, disjointed bones, and a heart melting like wax. Together they convey a collapse of strength and steadiness under distress. The verse should not be treated as a clinical diagnosis or a set of physical details from which to reconstruct an unnamed event. Its comparisons let the speaker say how completely the danger has affected them. The artwork uses spilled water and softened wax as symbols; these objects are artistic choices rather than objects reported at the scene. The poem continues to address this distress to God instead of hiding it.
verses.contextTitle: Bodily language within the encircling danger
verses.context: The open jaws of verse 13 are followed by the speaker’s water-and-wax comparisons. Verse 15 continues with dryness, thirst and the dust of death. These lines belong together as the lament’s expression of profound physical vulnerability.
explore: Poured out like water
The image evokes strength that seems unable to hold together. It is a comparison voiced by the sufferer, not an instruction to surrender to those causing harm.
My heart is like wax
The melting image expresses inner collapse alongside bodily distress. A candle or lump of wax in the illustration is symbolic art, not a described object in the psalm.
verses.reflect: How does heavy distress affect your sense of strength or steadiness? What kind of gentle, practical care would be welcome today?
verses.alt: Water spills from a tipped clay bowl across pale stone beside softened beeswax in an empty shaded courtyard.

verses.title: Dry as a potsherd
verses.heading: Dryness and thirst bring the speaker’s mortality into view
verses.meaning: A dry fragment of pottery becomes the comparison for spent strength, and the tongue sticking to the mouth gives thirst an immediate bodily expression. The final address, You lay me in the dust of death, brings the complaint directly to God. It names the speaker’s sense of nearing death without explaining the cause of suffering or declaring that every illness is divine punishment. John 19:28 later reports Jesus saying that He is thirsty, within its own account of His death; that connection should not be presented as an explicit quotation of this verse. The psalm’s own next appeal asks God to come quickly as the speaker’s strength.
verses.contextTitle: From melting weakness to the dust of death
verses.context: Verse 14’s flowing and melting images give way to dryness in verse 15. The dust of death will return in verse 29’s wider view of human mortality. Verse 19, meanwhile, addresses God as Strength in a renewed urgent plea.
explore: Like a potsherd
The comparison uses a dry broken piece of pottery to express exhausted strength. The painting’s pottery remains an illustration of the image, not an archaeological reconstruction.
The dust of death
The speaker places the prospect of death within the prayer to God. The line does not give readers permission to pronounce a judgment on another sufferer.
verses.reflect: What do you need when you feel depleted rather than strong? How might you make room for both an honest prayer and a concrete act of care?
verses.alt: A dry broken clay cup and pottery fragments lie on pale cracked earth beneath subdued distant hills.

verses.title: Encircled and wounded
verses.heading: The lament names human opponents beside the surrounding dogs
verses.meaning: Dogs surround the speaker, and the next clause explicitly names a band of evil men encircling them. The animal imagery and the human threat stand together in the lament. The bundled BSB then says that they have pierced the speaker’s hands and feet; those exact words remain Scripture and must not be softened or replaced by the illustration. The verse does not identify the opponents or describe a particular method of inflicting the wounds. Christian readers may hear it alongside the Gospel accounts of Jesus’ crucifixion, while distinguishing that later reading from an invented biography for the psalm’s speaker. No ethnic or religious group is named here as the target of blame.
verses.contextTitle: Enclosure returns, followed by the onlookers’ stare
verses.context: Verse 16 repeats the enclosure of verse 12 with dogs and a human band. Verse 17 continues with bodily vulnerability and staring onlookers. Verse 20 will ask for rescue from the power of wild dogs, keeping the image within the prayer’s movement.
explore: A band of evil men
The psalm explicitly names human opponents here but supplies no names or collective identity. The threatening animals do not establish who those people were.
My hands and feet
The BSB wording describes wounds without specifying their mechanism. The symbolic dogs in the watercolor illustrate enclosure, not the whole content of the verse.
A later Christian connection
Matthew 27:35 and John 19:18 describe Jesus’ crucifixion in their own narratives. Reading those accounts alongside this line does not require inventing the psalm’s original occasion.
verses.reflect: What is it like to have the seriousness of someone’s suffering overlooked? What response would take their pain seriously while preserving their dignity?
verses.alt: Several wary wild dogs stand around an empty narrow path beside a closed stone gateway, without wounds or a human figure.
